		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<a name="Item1"></a><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;color:#000000;">ITEM 1. BUSINESS</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;color:#000000;">General</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Guaranty Bancorp (the &#x201C;Company&#x201D;) is</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> a bank holding company registered under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> (the &#x201C;BHC Act&#x201D;) and headquartered in Colorado</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> The Company&#x2019;s</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> principal business is to serve as a holding company for our bank subsidiary, Guaranty Bank and Trust Company </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">referred to as </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;Guaranty Bank&#x201D; or &#x201C;Bank&#x201D;.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">References to the &#x201C;Company&#x201D;, &#x201C;us&#x201D;, &#x201C;we&#x201D; and &#x201C;our&#x201D; refer to Guaranty Bancorp on a consolidated basis. References to &#x201C;Guaranty Bancorp&#x201D; or to the &#x201C;holding company&#x201D; refer to the parent company on a stand-alone basis.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">At December 31, 201</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">6</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, we had total assets </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">of $3.4 billion, net loans of $2.5 billion, deposits of $2.7 billion and stockholders&#x2019; equity of $352.4 million, and we operated</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> 32</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> branches and two investment management firms in Colorado through our bank subsidiary, Guaranty Bank.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Guaranty Bancorp was incorporated in 2004 in </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the state of </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Delaware under the name Centennial C Corp</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">.,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and in 2004 and 2005</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">acquired several banking institutions and other entities, including </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Bank. By 2008, all of the entities acquired were either ultimately merged into either Guaranty Bancorp or </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> Bank or divested.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In 2008,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> the Company changed its name from Centennial Bank Holdings, Inc. to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">its current name, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Guaranty Bancorp.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Since </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">January 1, 2008, we have had a single bank subsidiary</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. The Bank is the sole member of </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">several </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">l</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">imited liability companies that hold real estate</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and the sole owner of two</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> investment </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">management</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> firm</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Private Capital Management LLC (&#x201C;PCM&#x201D;) and Cherry Hills Investment Advisors, Inc. (&#x201C;CHIA&#x201D;).</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> 2012, Guaranty Bank purchased substantially all of the assets of P</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">rivate Capital Management Inc.,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> a Denver-based firm providing investment </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">management</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and financial planning services to wealthy individuals </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">since 1994</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> 2014, Guaranty Bank purchased substantially all of the assets of Cherry Hills Investment Advisors LLC, a Greenwood Village-based firm providing investment management and financial planning services to individuals and families since 2009.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">On March 16, 2016, the Company entered into an Agreement and Plan of Reorganization (the &#x201C;Merger Agreement&#x201D;) with Home State Bancorp (&#x201C;Home State&#x201D;), the parent company of Home State Bank, a Colorado state chartered bank headquartered in Loveland, Colorado whereby Home State would merge into the Company. The transaction closed on September 8, 2016 with an aggregate transaction value of $152.5 million. With the acquisition, the Company increased its market share in Colorado northern </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">F</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ront </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">R</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ange markets and gain</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ed</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> the ability to provide customers with additional conveniences, including an expanded branch and ATM network. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;color:#000000;">Business </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:24.45pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The Bank provides </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">comprehensive </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">banking and other financial services including commercial and industrial, real estate, construction</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">consumer</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">loans throughout its targeted Colorado markets to consumers and small to medium-sized business</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">es</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, including the owners and employees of those businesses. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In addition to loans and depository services, t</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">he Bank also provide</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> wealth management </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">solutions</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, including </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">trust and</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> investment management services. Substantially all loans are secured by specific items of collateral, including business assets, consumer assets and commercial and residential real estate. Commercial loans are expected to be repaid from cash flow from business operations. There are no significant concentrations of loans to any one industry or </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">borrower. T</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">he </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">borrowers&#x2019; </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ability to repay their loans is generally dependent on the real estate market and general economic conditions prevailing in Colorado, among other factors.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:24.45pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">We concentrate our lending activities in the following principal areas:</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Commercial Loans: </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Our commercial and industrial loan portfolio is comprised of operating loans secured by business assets. The portfolio is not concentrated in any particular industry.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">We classify loans by </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">borrowers&#x2019; intended purpose for the loan rather than the underlying collateral.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Therefore, we include loans </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			<font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;">4</font><font style="display: inline;"></font>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div><hr size="3" style="color:#999999" width="100%" align="center"></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			<a href="#TableofContents"><font style="display: inline;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">within this portfolio that are collateralized with various assets, including real estate. Repayment of secured commercial and industrial loans depends substantially on the borrower&#x2019;s underlying business, financial condition and cash flows, as well as the sufficiency of the collateral.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Compared to real estate, the collateral </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">securing these loans </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">may be more difficult to monitor, evaluate and sell. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Economic conditions can significantly affect such risks.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Commercial and Residential Real Estate Loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">: This portfolio is mostly comprised of loans secured by commercial and residential real estate. The commercial real estate portfolio generally consists of owner-occupied, retail and industrial, office and multi-family properties. Commercial real estate and multi-family loans typically involve </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">one or more loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">a &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">single </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">sponsor</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> or groups of related </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">sponsor</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s. Since payments on these loans are often dependent on the successful operation or management of the properties</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> securing the loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, as well as the business and financial condition of the borrower, repayment of such loans may be subject to adverse conditions in the real estate market, adverse economic conditions or changes in applicable government regulations. If the</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> borrower is unable to obtain or renew </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">leases </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">for the underlying premises, causing a decline in cash flow from the property, the bo</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">rrower&#x2019;s ability to repay the loan may be impaired. Residential real estate is comprised of residential mortgages, primarily </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">jumbo mortgages </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">and home equity lines </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">of credit </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">to customers in our markets. Home equity lines </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">of credit </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">are underwritten in a manner such that they result in credit risk that is substantially similar to that of residential mortgage loans. Nevertheless, home equity lines have greater credit risk than residential mortgage loans because they </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">can be</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> secured by mortgages that are subordinated to the existing first mortgage on the property, which we may or may not hold, and they are not covered by private mortgage insurance.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Construction Loans: </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Our construction loan portfolio is comprised of investor</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">-</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">develope</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">r</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and owner-occupied properties and single-family residential development properties. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Investor-developer properties include</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> loans for the construction of commercial buildings, which are primarily income-producing properties. The repayment of construction loans is dependent upon the successful and timely completion of the construction of the subject property, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">which may additionally include achievement of stabilized occupancy, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">as well as the sale of the property to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">a &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">third part</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">y &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">or the availability of permanent financing upon completion of all improvements. Construction loans expose us to the risk that improvements will not be completed on time and in accordance with specifications and projected costs. Construction delays, the financial impairment of the builder, interest rate increases or economic downturn may further impair the borrower&#x2019;s ability to repay the loan. In addition, the ultimate sale or rental of the property may not occur as anticipated.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Installment Loans to Individuals and Other Consumer Loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">: This category includes miscellaneous consumer loans including overdraft protection</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> lines</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">of</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">credit</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and other consumer loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. Consumer loans may be unsecured or secured by rapidly deprecia</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ting</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> assets. Repossessed collateral for a defaulted consumer loan may not provide an adequate source of repayment for the outstanding loan and the remaining deficiency may not warrant further substantial collection efforts against the borrower. In addition, consumer loan collections are dependent on the borrower&#x2019;s continued financial stability, which can be adversely affected by job loss, divorce, illness or personal bankruptcy. Furthermore, the application of various federal and state laws, including federal and state bankruptcy and insolvency laws, may limit the amount </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">that</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">we </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">can recover on such loans.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Small Business Administration Loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">: Our Small Business Administration (&#x201C;SBA&#x201D;) portfolio consists of SBA guaranteed and other SBA-related loans. The guaranteed loans are for qualifying business purposes with maturity dates ranging </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">from </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">seven</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> to 25 years</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The SBA guarantees up to 90% of the financing for these types of loans. The SBA-related loans are originated in partnership with the SBA under the SBA&#x2019;s 504 </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">loan </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">program primarily on owner-occupied commercial real estate.</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 28.8pt;text-indent:7.2pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In addition, we provide traditional deposit accounts such as demand, interest-bearing demand, NOW, money market, IRA, time deposits and savings accounts. Our certificate of deposit customers primarily represent local relationships. Our branch network enables us to offer a full range of deposits, loans and personalized services to our targeted commercial and consumer customers.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;">Our</font><font style="display: inline;"> philosophy </font><font style="display: inline;">is to provide</font><font style="display: inline;"> relationship banking; offering a broad array of personalized financial products with highly responsive and exceptional customer service. We are a community bank that serves Colorado by providing sound financial solutions to customers through experienced, engaged and empowered employees. Our vision statement expands on this by stating that we want to be recognized as a trusted financial partner where </font>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Our strategy to build a profitable, community-banking franchise along the Colorado Front Range spanning from Castle Rock to Fort Collins has not changed over the past several years. The strategy for serving our target markets is the delivery of a finely-focused set of value-added products and services that satisfy the primary needs of our customers, emphasizing superior service and relationships as opposed to transaction volume or low pricing. As a locally managed banking institution, we believe we are able to react more quickly to customers&#x2019; needs and provide a superior level of customer service compared to larger regional and super-regional banks. </font>

Colorado&#x2019;s Front Range has a regional economy that is a diverse mix of advanced technology, tourism, manufacturing, service firms, government, education, retail, small business, construction and agriculture.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;color:#000000;">Competition </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The banking business in Colorado is highly competitive. The market is characterized by a number of large financial institutions </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">each </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">with a large number of offices</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and numerous small to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">medium</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">-sized community banks and credit unions. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In addition, non-bank entities in both the public and private sectors seeking to raise capital through the issuance and sale of debt or equity securities also provide competition for us in the acquisition of deposits. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">We also compete with brokerage firms, investment advisors, money market funds and issuers of other money market instruments. In recent years, increased competition has also developed from specialized finance and non-finance companies</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, some of which are not subject to the same regulatory requirements to which we are subject,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> that offer wholesale finance, credit card and other consumer finance services, including online banking services and personal finance software. Additionally, we expect competition to intensify among financial services companies due to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">mergers and </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">acquisition of institutions within our market area by other competing, out-of-state financial institutions. Competition for deposit and loan products remains strong from both banking and non-banking firms and this competition directly affects the rates and the terms </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">that we must offer </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">on</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> our products to remain competitive in the marketplace</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. In order to compete in our primary service area, we utilize to the fullest extent possible the flexibility that our community bank status permits, including </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">providing </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">an emphasis on specialized services, local promotional activity and personal contacts.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Technological innovation continues to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">increase</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> competition in </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">financial services markets. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">For example, t</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">echnolog</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">y has m</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ade it possible for non-depository institutions to offer customers automated transfer payment services previously limited to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">those offered as </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">traditional banking products. In addition, customers now expect a choice of several delivery systems and channels, including telephone, mail, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">online</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, automated teller machines (ATMs), debit cards, point-of-sale transactions, automated clearing house transactions (ACH), remote deposit, mobile banking via telephone or wireless devices and in-store branches.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Consolidation in the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">financial </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">services industry and the resulting economies of scale, as well as increasing costs associated with regulatory compliance, have</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> placed additional pressure on banks to consolidate their</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">operations, reduce expenses and increase revenues to remain competitive. In addition, competition has intensified due to federal and state interstate banking laws, which permit banking organizations to expand geographically with fewer restrictions than in the past. These laws allow out-of-state banks to establish or expand banking operations in our market. The competitive environment is also significantly impacted by federal and state legislation that makes it easier for non-bank financial institutions to compete with us.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;color:#000000;">Supervision and Regulation </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">General </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Banking is a complex, highly regulated industry. Consequently, the performance of the Company and the Bank can be affected not only by management decisions and general and local economic conditions, but also by the statutes </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">enacted</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> by, and the regulations and policies of, various governmental regulatory authorities. These authorities include, but are not limited to, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (the &#x201C;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201D;)</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, the Colorado Division of Banking</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> (the &#x201C;CDB&#x201D;), the Internal Revenue Service, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (the &#x201C;CFPB&#x201D;) </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">and state taxing authorities. The effect of these statutes, regulations and policies and any changes to any of them can be significant and cannot be predicted.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The primary goals of the bank regulatory scheme are to maintain a safe and sound banking system and to facilitate the conduct of sound monetary policy. In furtherance of these goals, the U.S. Congress and the State of Colorado have created several largely autonomous regulatory agencies </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">that oversee, and have </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">enacted numerous laws that govern banks, bank holding companies and the banking industry. The system of supervision and regulation applicable to the Company and the Bank establishes a comprehensive framework for the</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> entities&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> respective operations and is intended primarily for the protection of the Bank&#x2019;s depositors and the public, rather than the stockholders and creditors. The following summarize</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> some of the materially relevant laws, rules and regulations governing banks and bank holding companies, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">including the Company and the Bank, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">but does not purport to be a complete summary of all applicable laws, rules and regulations governing banks and bank holding companies</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> or the Company or the Bank</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. The descriptions are qualified in their entirety by reference to the specific </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">statutes, regulations and policies </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">discussed. </font><font style="display: inline;">Any change in applicable laws, regulations or regulatory policies may have a material effect on our businesses, operations and prospects. We are unable to predict the nature or extent of the effects that economic controls or new federal or state legislation may have on our business and earnings in the future.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Regulatory Agencies </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Guaranty Bancorp is a legal entity separate and distinct from its bank subsidiary, Guaranty Bank. As a bank holding company, Guaranty Bancorp is regulated under the B</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">HC Act</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and is subject to inspection, examination and supervision by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, or the Federal Reserve Board. Guaranty Bancorp is also under the jurisdiction of the SEC and is subject to the disclosure and regulatory requirements of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> (the &#x201C;Exchange Act&#x201D;)</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. Guaranty Bancorp is listed on The NASDAQ </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Global Select M</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">arket (</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Nasdaq</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201D;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">) under the trading symbol &#x201C;GBNK,&#x201D; and is subject to the rules of Nasdaq for listed companies.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">As a Colorado-chartered bank, the Bank is subject to supervision, periodic examination and regulation by the CDB. As a member of the Federal Reserve System, the Bank is also subject to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">supervision, periodic examination and regulation by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, or the Federal Reserve. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In addition, the Bank is subject to certain rules and regulations of the CFPB, and PCM and CHIA are subject to the disclosure and regulatory requirements of the Investment Advisors Act of 1940, as amended. </font><font style="display: inline;">The deposits of the Bank are insured by the FDIC</font><font style="display: inline;"> up to certain established limits</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">On July 21, 2010, President Obama signed into law the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (the &#x201C;Dodd-Frank Act&#x201D;), which implement</font><font style="display: inline;">ed and continues to implement</font><font style="display: inline;"> significant changes to the regulation of the financial services industry</font><font style="display: inline;">. &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The effects of the Dodd-Frank Act have been far-reaching, and many </font><font style="display: inline;">aspects of the Dodd-Frank Act remain subject to rulemaking by various regulatory agencies and will take effect over several years, making it difficult to anticipate the overall financial impact on the Company, its customers or the financial industry more generally. </font>
		</p>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div><hr size="3" style="color:#999999" width="100%" align="center"></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			<a href="#TableofContents"><font style="display: inline;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;">Provisions in the legislation that require revisions to the capital requirements of the Company and the Bank could require the Company and the Bank to seek additional sources of capital in the future.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Bank Holding Company Regulations Applicable to Guaranty Bancorp</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The BHC Act and other federal laws subject bank holding companies to particular restrictions on the types of activities in which they may engage, and to a range of supervisory requirements and activities, including regulatory enforcement actions for violations of laws and regulations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Permitted activities</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. Generally, bank holding companies are prohibited under the BHC Act from engaging in or acquiring direct or indirect control of more than 5% of the voting shares of any company engaged in any activity other than (i)&nbsp;banking or managing or controlling banks or (ii)&nbsp;an activity that the Federal Reserve Board determines to be so closely related to banking as to be a proper incident to the business of banking. The Federal Reserve Board has the authority to require a bank holding company to terminate an activity or terminate control of or liquidate or divest certain subsidiaries or affiliates when the Federal Reserve Board believes the activity or the control of the subsidiary or affiliate constitutes a significant risk to the financial safety, soundness or stability of any of its banking subsidiaries.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">A bank holding company that qualifies and elects to become a financial holding company is permitted to engage in additional activities that are financial in nature or incidental or complementary to financial activity. We currently have no plans to make a financial holding company election.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Sound banking practices</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. Bank holding companies and their non-banking subsidiaries are prohibited from engaging in activities that represent unsafe and unsound banking practices. For example, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">under certain circumstances </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the Federal Reserve Board&#x2019;s Regulation Y requires a holding company to give the Federal Reserve Board prior notice of any redemption or repurchase of its own equity securities if the consideration to be paid, together with the consideration paid for any repurchases in the preceding year, is equal to 10% or more of the company&#x2019;s consolidated net worth. The Federal Reserve Board may oppose the transaction if it believes that the transaction would constitute an unsafe or unsound practice or would violate a</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">regulation. As another example, a holding company </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">is prohibited from impairing </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">its subsidiary bank&#x2019;s soundness by causing </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the bank</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> to make funds available to non-banking subsidiaries or their customers if the Federal Reserve believe</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> it not prudent to do so. The Federal Reserve Board </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">has the power to asses</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s civil money penalties for knowing </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">or </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">reckless </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">violations</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, if the activities </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">leading to a violation </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">caused a substantial loss to a depository institution. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Potential</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> penalties </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">are</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> as high as $1,000,000 for each day the activity continues.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Source of Strength</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. In accordance with Federal Reserve Board policy, the holding company is expected to act as a source of financial </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">and managerial </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">strength to the Bank. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Under this policy, the holding company is expected to commit resources to support its bank subsidiary, including at times when the holding company may not be in a financial position to provide it. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">As discussed below, the holding company could be required to guarantee the capital plan of the Bank if it becomes undercapitalized for purposes of banking regulations. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Any capital loans by a bank holding company to its subsidiary bank are subordinate in right of payment to deposits and to certain other indebtedness of such subsidiary bank. The BHC Act provides that, in the event of a bank holding company&#x2019;s bankruptcy, any commitment by the bank holding company to a federal bank regulatory agency to maintain the capital of a bank subsidiary will be assumed by the bankruptcy trustee and entitled to priority of payment.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Regulatory agencies have </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">promulga</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ted</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> regulations to increase the capital requirements for bank holding companies to a level that matches those of banking institutions.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Anti-tying restrictions</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. Bank holding companies and affiliates are prohibited from tying the provision of services, such as extensions of credit, to other services offered by a holding company or its affiliates.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Acquisitions</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The BHC Act, the Bank Merger Act, the Colorado Banking Code and other federal and state statutes regulate acquisitions of commercial banks and their holding companies. The BHC Act generally limits acquisitions by bank holding companies to commercial banks and companies engaged in activities that the Federal Re</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">serve Board has determined to be so closely related to banking as to be a proper incident thereto. The BHC Act requires every bank holding company to obtain the prior approval of the Federal Reserve before (i)&nbsp;acquiring more than 5% of the voting stock of any bank or other bank holding company, (ii)&nbsp;acquiring all or substantially all of the assets of any bank or bank holding company, or (iii)&nbsp;merging or consolidating with any other bank holding company.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			<font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;">8</font><font style="display: inline;"></font>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div><hr size="3" style="color:#999999" width="100%" align="center"></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			<a href="#TableofContents"><font style="display: inline;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In reviewing applications seeking approval of merger and acquisition transactions, the bank regulatory authorities </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">generally co</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">nsider, among other things, the competitive effect and public benefits of the transactions, the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">financial and managerial resources and future prospects of the combined organization (including </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the capital position of the combined organization), the applicant&#x2019;s performance record under the Community Reinvestment Act (see the section captioned &#x201C;Community Reinvestment Act&#x201D; included elsewhere in this item), fair housing laws and the effectiveness of the subject organizations in combating money laundering activities.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The Company is also subject to the Change in Bank Control Act of 1978 (the &#x201C;Control Act&#x201D;) and related Federal Reserve Board regulations, which provide that any person who proposes to acquire </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">at least </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">10% (but less than 25%) of any class of a bank holding company&#x2019;s voting securities is presumed to control the company (unless the company is not publicly held and some other shareholder owns a greater percentage of voting stock). Any person who would be presumed to acquire control or who proposes to acquire control of more than 25% of any class of a bank holding company&#x2019;s </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">voting </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">securities, or who proposes to acquire actual control, must provide the Federal Reserve Board with </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">at least </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">60 day</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;font-size:5pt;vertical-align:super;line-height:100%">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">prior written notice of the acquisition. The Federal Reserve Board may disapprove a proposed acquisition if (i)&nbsp;it would result in adverse competitive effects, (ii)&nbsp;the financial condition of the acquiring person might jeopardize the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">target </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">institution&#x2019;s financial stability or prejudice the interests of depositors, (iii)&nbsp;the competence, experience or integrity of any acquiring person indicates that the proposed acquisition would not be in the best interests of the depositors or the public, or (iv)&nbsp;the acquiring person fails to provide all of the information required by the Federal Reserve Board. Any proposed acquisition of the voting securities of a bank holding company that is subject to approval under the BHC Act is not subject to the Control Act notice requirements. Any company that proposes to acquire &#x201C;control&#x201D;, as those terms are defined in the BHC Act and Federal Reserve Board regulations, of a bank holding company or to acquire 25% or more of any class of voting securities of a bank holding company would be required to seek the Federal Reserve Board&#x2019;s prior approval under the BHC Act to become a bank holding company.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Dividends</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Dividends from the Bank</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">are </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the holding company&#x2019;s </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">principal source of cash r</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">evenues</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. Our ear</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">nings and activities are affected by legislation, by regulations and by local legislative and administrative bodies and decisions of courts in the jurisdictions in which we conduct business. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">T</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">hese include limitations on the ability of the Bank to pay dividends to the holding company and our ability to pay dividends to our stockholders. It is the policy of the Federal Reserve Board that bank holding companies should pay cash dividends on common stock only out of income available over the past year and only if prospective earnings retention is consistent with the organization&#x2019;s expected future needs and financial condition. The policy provides that bank holding companies should not maintain a level of cash </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">dividends that undermines the bank holding company&#x2019;s ability to serve as a source of strength to its banking subsidiary. Consistent with such policy, </font><font style="display: inline;">a banking organization should have comprehensive policies on dividend payments that clearly articulate the organization&#x2019;s objectives and approaches for maintaining a strong capital position and achieving the objectives of the policy statement.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In 2009, the Federal Reserve Board issued a supervisory letter providing greater clarity to its policy statement on the payment of dividends by bank holding companies. In this letter, the Federal Reserve Board stated that </font><font style="display: inline;">when a holding company&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;">s board of directors is deciding on the level of dividends to declare, it should consider, among other factors: (i)&nbsp;overall asset quality, potential need to increase reserves and write down assets, and concentrations of credit; (ii)&nbsp;potential for unanticipated losses and declines in asset values; (iii)&nbsp;implicit and explicit liquidity and credit commitments, including off-balance sheet and contingent liabilities; (iv)&nbsp;quality and level of current and prospective earnings, including earnings capacity under a number of plausible economic scenarios; (v)&nbsp;current and prospective cash flow and liquidity; (vi)&nbsp;ability to serve as an ongoing source of financial and managerial strength to depository institution subsidiaries insured by the FDIC, including the extent of double leverage</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:5pt;vertical-align:super;line-height:100%">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">and the condition of subsidiary depository institutions; (vii)&nbsp;other risks </font><font style="display: inline;">that affect the holding company&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;">s financial condition and are not fully captured in regulatory capital calculations; (viii)&nbsp;level, composition, and quality of capital; and (ix)&nbsp;ability to raise additional equity capital in prevailing marke</font><font style="display: inline;">t and economic conditions (the &#x201C;Dividend Factors&#x201D;</font><font style="display: inline;">). It is particularly important for a </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">bank holding company&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">board of directors to ensure that the dividend level is prudent relative to the organization&#x2019;s financial position and is not based on overly optimistic earnings scenarios. In addition, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">a bank holding company&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s board of directors should strongly consider, after careful analysis of the Dividend Factors, reducing, deferring, or eliminating dividends when the quantity and quality of the holding company's earnings have declined or the holding company is experiencing other financial problems, or when the macroeconomic outlook for the holding company's primary profit centers has deteriorated. The Federal Reserve Board further stated that, as a general matter, a bank holding company should eliminate, defer or significantly reduce its distributions if: (</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">a</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">) its net income is not sufficient to fully fund the dividends, (</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">b</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">) its prospective rate of earnings retention is not consistent with its capital needs and overall current and prospective financial condition, or (</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">c</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">)&nbsp;it will not meet, or is in danger of not meeting, its minimum regulatory capital adequacy ratios. Failure to do so could result in a supervisory finding that the bank holding company is operating in an unsafe and unsound manner.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;">9</font><font style="display: inline;"></font>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div><hr size="3" style="color:#999999" width="100%" align="center"></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			<a href="#TableofContents"><font style="display: inline;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;">Additionally, as discussed above, the Federal Reserve </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Board </font><font style="display: inline;">possesses enforcement powers over bank holding companies and their non-bank subsidiaries </font><font style="display: inline;">with which it can </font><font style="display: inline;">prevent or remedy actions that represent unsafe or unsound practices, or violations of applicable statutes and regulations. Among these powers is the ability to proscribe the payment of </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">dividends</font><font style="display: inline;"> by bank</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;"> and bank holding companies.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;text-decoration:underline;">Stock Redemptions and Repurchases</font><font style="display: inline;">. It is an essential principle of safety and soundn</font><font style="display: inline;">ess that a banking organization&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;">s redemption and repurchases of regulatory capital instruments, including common stock, from investors be consistent with the organization&#x2019;s current and prospective capital needs. In assessing such needs, the board of directors and management of a bank holding company should consider the Dividend</font><font style="display: inline;"> Factors discussed above under &#x201C;Dividends&#x201D;</font><font style="display: inline;">. The risk-based capital rule directs bank holding companies to consult with the Federal Reserve before redeeming any equity or other capital instrument included in Tier&nbsp;1 or Tier&nbsp;2 capital prior to stated maturity, if such redemption could have a material effect on the level or composition of the organization&#x2019;s capital base. Bank holding companies </font><font style="display: inline;">that are </font><font style="display: inline;">experiencing financial weaknesses, or that are at significant risk of developing financial weaknesses, must consult with the appropriate Federal Reserve supervisory staff before redeeming or repurchasing common stock or other regulatory capital instruments for cash or other valuable consideration. Similarly, any bank holding company considering expansion, </font><font style="display: inline;">whether</font><font style="display: inline;"> through acquisitions or through </font><font style="display: inline;">organic growth and </font><font style="display: inline;">new activities, generally </font><font style="display: inline;">also </font><font style="display: inline;">must consult with the appropriate Federal Reserve supervisory staff before redeeming or repurchasing common stock or other regulatory capital instruments for cash or other valuable consideration. In evaluating the appropriat</font><font style="display: inline;">eness of a bank holding company&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;">s proposed redemption or repurchase of capital instruments, the Federal Reserve will consider the potential losses that the holding company may suffer from the prospective need to increase reserves and write down assets from continued asset deter</font><font style="display: inline;">ioration and the holding company&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;">s ability to raise additional common stock and other Tier&nbsp;1 capital to replace capital instruments th</font><font style="display: inline;">at are redeemed or repurchased.</font><font style="display: inline;"> A bank holding company must inform the Federal Reserve of a redemption or repurchase</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:5pt;vertical-align:super;line-height:100%">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">of common stock or perpetual preferred stock for cash or other value resulting in a net reduction of the ba</font><font style="display: inline;">nk holding company&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;">s outstanding amount of common stock or perpetual preferred stock below the amount of such capital instrument outstanding at the beginning of the quarter in which the redemption or repurchase occurs.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">In addition, a bank holding company must advise the Federal Reserve sufficiently in advance of such redemptions and repurchases to provide reasonable opportunity for supervisory review and possible objection should the Federal Reserve determine a transaction raises safety and soundness concerns.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Regulation&nbsp;Y requires that a bank holding company that is not well capitalized or well managed, or that is subject to any unresolved supervisory issues, provide prior notice to the Federal Reserve for any repurchase or redemption of its equity securities for cash or other value that would reduce by 10</font><font style="display: inline;">%</font><font style="display: inline;"> or more the holding company's consolidated net worth aggregated over the preceding 12-month period.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;text-decoration:underline;">Annual Reporting; Examinations</font><font style="display: inline;">. The holding company is required to file an annual report with the Federal Reserve Board, and such additional information as the Federal Reserve Board may require.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">The Federal Reserve Board may examine a bank holding company and any of its subsidiaries, and charge the company for the cost of such an examination.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;text-decoration:underline;">Imposition of Liability for Undercapitalized Subsidiaries</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">.</font><font style="display: inline;"> The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act of 1991 (&#x201C;FDICIA&#x201D;) requires bank regulators to take &#x201C;prompt corrective action&#x201D; to resolve problems associated with insured depository institutions. In the event an institution becomes &#x201C;undercapitalized,&#x201D; it must submit a capital restoration plan. The capital restoration plan will not be accepted by the regulators unless each company &#x201C;having control of&#x201D; the undercapitalized institution &#x201C;guarantees&#x201D; the subsidiary&#x2019;s compliance with the capital restoration plan until it becomes &#x201C;adequately capitalized.&#x201D; For purposes of this statute, the holding company has control of the Bank. Under FDICIA, the aggregate liability of all companies controlling a particular institution is limited to the lesser of five percent of the depository institution&#x2019;s total assets at the time it became undercapitalized or the amount necessary to bring the institution into compliance with applicable capital standards. FDICIA grants greater powers to bank regulators in situations where an institution becomes &#x201C;significantly&#x201D; or &#x201C;critically&#x201D; undercapitalized or fails to submit a capital restoration plan. For example, a bank holding company controlling such an institution can be required to obtain prior Federal Reserve Board approval of proposed distributions,</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">or might be required to consent to a merger or to divest the troubled institution or other affiliates.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Transactions with Affiliates</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The holding company and the Bank are </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">considered &#x201C;a</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ffiliates</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201D;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> of each other </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">under </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the Federal Reserve Act, and transactions between </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">such </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">affiliates are subject to certain restrictions, including compliance with Sections 23A and 23B of the Federal Reserve Act and their implementing regulations. Generally, Sections 23A and 23B: (1)&nbsp;limit the extent to which a financial institution or its subsidiaries may engage in covered transactions (a)&nbsp;with an affiliate (as defined in such sections) to an amount equal to 10% of such institution&#x2019;s capital and surplus, and (b)&nbsp;with all affiliates, in the aggregate to an amount equal to 20% of such capital and surplus; and </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		</p>
