		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">(2)&nbsp;require all transactions with an affiliate, whether or not covered transactions, to be on terms substantially the same, or at least as favorable to the institution or subsidiary, as the terms provided or that would be provided to a non-affiliate. The term &#x201C;covered transaction&#x201D; includes the making of loans, purchase of assets, issuance of a guarantee and other similar types of transactions.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;text-decoration:underline;">State Law Restrictions</font><font style="display: inline;">. As a Delaware corporation, the holding company is subject to certain limitations and restrictions under applicable Delaware corporate law. For example, state law restrictions in Delaware include limitations and restrictions relating to indemnification of directors, distributions and dividends to stockholders, transactions involving directors, officers or interested stockholders, maintenance of books, records, and minutes, and observance of certain corporate formalities.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Capital Adequacy and Prompt Corrective Action &#x2013; Guaranty Bancorp and Guaranty Bank</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The federal bank regulatory authorities&#x2019; risk-based capital guidelines were previously based upon the 1988 capital accord of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, or Basel I. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision is a committee of central banks and bank supervisors and regulators from the major industrialized countries that develops broad policy guidelines for use by each country&#x2019;s supervisors in determining the supervisory policies they apply. In 2004, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision published a new capital accord to replace Basel I, with an update in November 2005 (&#x201C;Basel II&#x201D;). Basel II provided two approaches for setting capital standards for credit risk &#x2014; an internal ratings-based approach tailored to individual institutions&#x2019; circumstances (which for many asset classes is itself broken into a &#x201C;foundation&#x201D; approach and an &#x201C;advanced or A-IRB&#x201D; approach, the availability of which is subject to additional restrictions) and a standardized approach that based risk weightings on external credit assessments to a much greater extent than permitted in previous risk-based capital guidelines. Basel II also set capital requirements for operational risk and refined the existing capital requirements for market risk exposures.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In July 2007, the U.S. banking and thrift agencies reached an agreement on the implementation of the capital adequacy regulations and standards based on Basel II. In November 2007, the agencies </font><font style="display: inline;">approved final rules to implement the new risk-based capital requirements in the United States for large, internationally active banking organizations, or &#x201C;core banks&#x201D; </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">- defined as those with consolidated total assets of $250 billion or more or consolidated on-balance sheet foreign exposures of $10 billion or more. The final rule was effective as of April</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">1,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">2008. We are not a core bank and do not apply the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Basel</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> II approach to computing risk-weighted assets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In response to the economic and financial industry crisis that began in 2008, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and their </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">oversight body - the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS) &#x2013; set out in late 2009 to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">work on </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">global initiatives to strengthen the financial regulatory system</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. In July 2010, the GHOS agreed on key design elements and in September 2010 agreed to transition and implementation measures. This work is known as Basel III, and it is designed to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">strengthen the regulation, supervision and risk management of the banking sector. In particular, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Basel III</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> strengthen</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">existing capital requirements and introduce</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> a global liquidity standard. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In June&nbsp;2012, the Federal Reserve Board, the FDIC and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (the &#x201C;OCC&#x201D;) jointly issued three notices of proposed rulemaking (&#x201C;NPRs&#x201D;) to, among other things</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">implement the Basel III minimum capital requirements. Following the receipt of comment letters from multiple U.S. financial institutions, on November&nbsp;9, 2012, the Federal Reserve Board, the FDIC, and the OCC indefinitely delayed the start date for the Basel III capital requirements and stated that they did not expect the final rules&nbsp;to implement the Basel III capital requirements to be in effect on January&nbsp;1, 2013, the initial deadline. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In July 2013, the Federal Reserve Board, the FDIC and OCC issued two final interim rules to implement the Basel III capital reforms and the rules began p</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">has</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ing</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">-in in 2015, depending on the size of the financial institution. For more on Basel III and its potential effect on us, see item 1A &#x201C;Risk Factors&#x201D;. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The Federal Deposit Insurance Act, as amended (&#x201C;FDIA&#x201D;), requires, among other things, that federal banking agencies take &#x201C;prompt corrective action&#x201D; with respect to depository institutions that do not meet minimum capital requirements. The FDIA sets forth the following five capital tiers: &#x201C;well capitalized,&#x201D; &#x201C;adequately capitalized,&#x201D; &#x201C;undercapitalized,&#x201D; &#x201C;significantly undercapitalized&#x201D; and &#x201C;critically undercapitalized.&#x201D; A depository institution&#x2019;s capital tier will depend upon how its capital levels compare with various relevant capital measures and certain other factors, as established by regulation. The relevant capital measures are the total capital ratio, the Tier 1 capital ratio</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> the leverage ratio</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and a new ratio requirement under Basel III, the common equity Tier I capital ratio</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Under the regulations adopted by the federal regulatory authorities, a bank </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">is</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">: (i)</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;well capitalized&#x201D; if the institution has a </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">total risk-based capital ratio of 10.0% or greater, a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 6.5% or greater, a Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio of 8.0% or greater, and a leverage ratio of 5.0% or greater, and is not subject </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			<font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;">11</font><font style="display: inline;"></font>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div><hr size="3" style="color:#999999" width="100%" align="center"></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			<a href="#TableofContents"><font style="display: inline;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">to any order or written directive by any such regulatory authority to meet and maintain a specific capital level for any capital measure; (ii)</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;adequately capitalized&#x201D; if the institution has a total risk-based capital ratio of 8.0% or greater, a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5% or greater, a Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio of 6.0% or greater and a leverage ratio of 4.0% or greater and is not &#x201C;well capitalized&#x201D;; (iii)</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;undercapitalized&#x201D; if the institution has a total risk-based capital ratio that is less than 8.0%, a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of less than 4.5%, a Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio of less than 6.0% or a leverage ratio of less than 4.0%; (iv)&nbsp;&#x201C;significantly undercapitalized&#x201D; if the institution has a total risk-based capital ratio of less than 6.0%, a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of less than 3.0%, a Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio of less than 4.0% or a leverage ratio of less than 3.0%; and (v)</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;critically undercapitalized&#x201D; if the institution&#x2019;s tangible equity is equal to or less than 2.0% of average quarterly tangible assets. An institution may be downgraded to, or deemed to be in, a capital category that is lower than indicated by its capital ratios if it is determined to be in an unsafe or unsound condition or if it receives an unsatisfactory examination rating with respect to certain matters. A bank&#x2019;s capital category is determined solely for the purpose of applying prompt corrective action regulations, and the capital category may not constitute an accurate representation of the bank&#x2019;s overall financial condition or prospects for other purposes.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The final rules also established a &#x201C;capital conservation buffer&#x201D; of 2.5% above the regulatory minimum capital ratios, and when fully effective in 2019, will result in the following minimum ratios: (i) a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 7.0%; (ii)&nbsp;a Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio of 8.5%; and (iii) a total capital ratio of 10.5%. The new capital conservation buffer requirement began phasing in January 2016 at 0.625% of risk-weighted assets and will increase each year until fully implemented in January 2019. An institution is subject to limitations on paying dividends, engaging in share repurchases, and paying discretionary bonuses if its buffer level falls below the required buffer amount. These limitations will establish a maximum percentage of eligible retained income that can be utilized for such activities. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The FDIA generally prohibits a depository institution from making any capital distributions (including payment of a dividend) or paying any management fee to its parent holding company if the depository institution would thereafter be undercapitalized. Undercapitalized institutions are subject to growth limitations and are required to submit a capital restoration plan</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> to the FDIC</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. The agencies may not accept such a plan without determining, among other things, that the plan is based on realistic assumptions and is likely to succeed in restoring the depository institution&#x2019;s capital. In addition, for a capital restoration plan to be acceptable, the depository institution&#x2019;s parent holding company must guarantee that the institution will comply with such capital restoration plan. The aggregate liability of the parent holding company is limited to the lesser of (i) an amount equal to 5.0% of the depository institution&#x2019;s total assets at the time it became undercapitalized and (ii) the amount which is necessary (or would have been necessary) to bring the institution into compliance with all capital standards applicable with respect to such institution as of the time it fails to comply with the plan. If a depository institution fails to submit an acceptable plan, it is treated as if it is &#x201C;significantly undercapitalized.&#x201D;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;Significantly undercapitalized&#x201D; depository institutions may be subject to a number of requirements and restrictions, including orders to sell sufficient voting stock to become &#x201C;adequately capitalized,&#x201D; requirements to reduce total assets, and cessation of receipt of deposits from correspondent banks. &#x201C;Critically undercapitalized&#x201D; institutions are subject to the appointment of a receiver or conservator.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Both Guaranty Bank and Guaranty Bancorp have always maintained the capital ratios and leverage ratio above the levels to be considered quantitatively well-capitalized. For information regarding the capital ratios and leverage ratio of the Company and the Bank a</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s of </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">December 31, 201</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">6</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">December 31, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">201</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">5</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, see the discussion under the section captioned &#x201C;Capital</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> Resources</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201D; included in Item 7, &#x201C;Management&#x2019;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201D; &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">and Note 2</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">1</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> &#x2014;Regulatory</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> Capital Matters in </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;Notes to Consolidated F</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">inancial </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">S</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">tatements</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201D;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> included in Item 8, &#x201C;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data&#x201D;, elsewhere in this report.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Banking Regulations Applicable to Guaranty Bank</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Branching</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. Colorado state law provides that a Colorado-chartered bank can establish a branch anywhere in Colorado provided that the branch is approved in advance by the </font><font style="display: inline;">C</font><font style="display: inline;">D</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">B.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The branch must also be approved by the Federal Reserve. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The approval process takes into account </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">a number of factors, including financial history, capital adequacy, earnings prospects, character of management, needs of the community and consistency with corporate powers. The Dodd-Frank Act also reduced any significant barriers to interstate branching.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Dividends</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">As a member of the Federal Reserve System, the Bank is subject to Regulation H, which, among other things, provides that a member bank may not declare or pay a dividend if the total of all dividends declared during the calendar year, including the proposed dividend, exceeds the sum of the bank&#x2019;s net income (as reportable </font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">in its Reports of Condition and Income) during the current calendar year and its retained net income for the prior two calendar years, unless the Federal Reserve has approved the dividend.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Regulation H also provides that a member bank may not declare or pay a dividend if the dividend would exceed the bank&#x2019;s undivided profits as reportable on its Reports of Condition and Income, unless the Federal Reserve and holders of at least two-thirds of the outstanding shares of each class of the bank&#x2019;s outstanding stock have approved the dividend. Additionally, there are potential additional restrictions and prohibitions if a bank were to be less than well-capitalized.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">As a Colorado state-chartered bank, the Bank is subject to limitations under Colorado law on the payment of dividends. The Colorado Banking Code provides that a bank may declare dividends from retained earnings and other components of capital specifically approved by the Banking Board so long as the declaration is made in compliance with rules established by the Banking Board.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Deposit Insurance</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The deposits of the Bank are insured up to applicable limits by the Deposit Insurance Fund </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">(</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">DIF</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201D;)</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> of the FDIC and are subject to deposit insurance assessments to maintain the DIF. The FDIC utilizes a risk-based assessment system that imposes insurance premiums based upon a risk matrix that takes into account a bank&#x2019;s capital level and supervisory rating. Risk Category I is the lowest risk category while Risk Category IV is the highest </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">risk category.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In 2010, the Dodd-Frank Act revised certain statutes governing the FDIC&#x2019;s management of the DIF. Among other things, the revisions raised the minimum fund reserve ratio from 1.15% to 1.35% and required the fund reserve ratio to reach 1.35% by September 30, 2020. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In August 2016, the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> announced that the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">fund</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> reserve ratio had surpassed 1.15% as of June&nbsp;30, 2016. As a result, beginning in the third quarter of 2016, the range of initial assessment rates for all institutions was adjusted downward and institutions with $10&nbsp;billion or more in assets were assessed a quarterly surcharge. The quarterly surcharge will continue to be assessed until such time as the reserve ratio reaches the statutory minimum of 1.35% required by the Dodd-Frank Act.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;The Company had $</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">3.4</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">billion </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">in total assets as of December 31, 2016 and therefore was not subject to the quarterly surcharge.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">At December 31, 2016, the Bank&#x2019;s total assessment rate was approximately three basis points.</font>

The FDIC may terminate deposit insurance if it determines the institution involved has engaged in or is engaging in unsafe or unsound banking practices, is in an unsafe or unsound condition, or has violated applicable laws, regulations or orders.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In the case of a Colorado-chartered bank, the termination of deposit insurance would result in the revocation of its charter.</font>

If an insured depository institution fails, insured and uninsured depositors, along with the FDIC, will have priority in payment ahead of unsecured, non-deposit creditors, including the parent bank holding company, with respect to any extensions of credit they have made to such insured depository institution.</font>

Under the CRA, each depository institution is required to help meet the credit needs of its market areas by, among other things, providing credit to low- and moderate-income individuals and communities. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">These factors are also considered in evaluating mergers, acquisitions and applications to open a branch or facility.</font><font style="display: inline;"> The applicable federal regulators regularly conduct CRA examinations to assess the performance of financial institutions and assign one of four ratings to the institution&#x2019;s records of meeting the credit needs of its community. Extensions of credit to such persons must: (</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">i</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">)&nbsp;be made on substantially the same terms, including interest rates and collateral, and follow credit underwriting procedures that are not less stringent than those prevailing at the time for comparable transactions with persons not covered by such restrictions and (</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ii</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">)&nbsp;not involve more than the normal risk of repayment or present other unfavorable features. Banks are also subject to certain lending limits and restrictions on overdrafts to such persons. A violation of these restrictions may result in the assessment of substantial civil monetary penalties on the affected bank or any officer, director, employee, agent or other person participating in the conduct of the affairs of that bank, the imposition of a cease and desist order, and other regulatory sanctions.</font>

In general, the guidelines establish two concentration levels.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">First, a concentration is deemed to exist if the institution&#x2019;s total construction, land development and other land loans represent 100 percent or more of total risk-based capital (&#x201C;CRE 1 Concentration&#x201D;).</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Second, a concentration will be deemed to exist if total loans for construction, land development and other land and loans secured by multifamily and non-owner occupied non-farm residential properties (excluding loans secured by owner-occ</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">upied properties) represent 300 percent</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> or more of total risk-based capital (&#x201C;CRE 2 Concentration&#x201D;) and the institution&#x2019;s commercial real estate loan portfolio has increased by 50 </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">percent or more during the prior 36 month period. As of December 31, 2016, the Bank&#x2019;s CRE 1 Concentration level was 40 percent and the Bank&#x2019;s CRE 2 </font>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">FDICIA</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> Under FDICIA, each federal banking agency has prescribed, by regulation, non-capital safety and soundness standards for institutions under its authority. These standards cover internal controls, information and internal audit systems, loan documentation, credit underwriting, interest rate exposure, asset growth, compensation, fees and benefits, such other operational and managerial standards as the agency determines to be appropriate, and standards for asset quality, earnings and stock valuation. An institution which fails to meet these standards must develop a plan acceptable to the agency, specifying the steps that the institution will take to meet the standards. Failure to submit or implement such a plan may subject the institution to regulatory sanctions.</font>

These limitations require disclosure of privacy policies to consumers and, in some circumstances, allow consumers to prevent disclosure of certain personal information to a nonaffiliated third party. The privacy provisions of the GLB Act affect how consumer information is transmitted through diversified financial companies and conveyed to outside vendors.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Anti-Money Laundering Initiatives and the USA Patriot Act</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">A major focus of governmental policy on financial institutions over the last decade has been combating money laundering and terrorist financing. The USA PATRIOT Act of 2001</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> &nbsp;(</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201C;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">USA Patriot Act</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#x201D;)</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, substantially broadened the scope of United States anti-money laundering laws and regulations by imposing significant new compliance and due diligence obligations, creating new crimes and penalties and expanding the extra-territorial jurisdiction of the United States. The U.S. Treasury Department has issued a number of regulations that apply various requirements of the USA Patriot Act to financial institutions such as the Bank. These regulations impose obligations on financial institutions to maintain appropriate policies, procedures and controls to detect, prevent and report money laundering and terrorist financing and to verify the identit</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ies</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> of their customers. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">F</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">inancial institution</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">s are also prohibited from entering into specified financial transactions and account relationships and must use enhanced due diligence procedures in their dealings with certain types of high-risk customers and implement a written customer identification program. Financial institutions must take certain steps to assist government agencies in detecting and preventing money </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">laundering and </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">report</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ing</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> certain types of suspicious transactions. Regulatory authorities routinely examine financial institutions for compliance with these obligations, and failure of a financial institution to maintain and implement adequate programs to combat money laundering and </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">terrorist financing, or to comply with all of the relevant laws or regulations, c</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">an</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> have serious legal and reputational consequences for the institution.</font>

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Office of Foreign Assets Control Regulation</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The United States has imposed economic sanctions that affect transactions with designated foreign countries, nationals and others. These are typically known as the &#x201C;OFAC&#x201D; rules based on their administration by the U.S. Treasury Department Office of Foreign Assets Control (&#x201C;OFAC&#x201D;). The OFAC-administered sanctions targeting countries take many different forms. Generally, however, they contain one or more of the following elements: (i) restrictions on trade with or investment in a sanctioned country, including prohibitions against direct or indirect imports from and exports to a sanctioned country and prohibitions on &#x201C;U.S. persons&#x201D; engaging in financial transactions relating to making investments in, or providing investment-related advice or assistance to, a sanctioned country; and (ii) a blocking of assets in which the government or specially designated nationals of the sanctioned country have an interest, by prohibiting transfers of property subject to U.S. jurisdiction (including property in the possession or control of U.S. persons). Blocked assets (e.g., property and bank deposits) cannot be paid out, withdrawn, set off or transferred in any manner without a license from OFAC.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> The Company is responsible for, among other things, blocking accounts of, and transactions with, such targets and countries, prohibiting unlicensed trade and financial transactions with them and reporting blocked transactions after their occurrence. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Failure to comply with these sanctions could have serious legal and reputational consequences.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;text-decoration:underline;">Other Laws and Regulations</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The Company is not only subject to federal laws applicable to it, it is also subject to the rules and regulations of the various federal agencies charged with the responsibility of implementing these federal laws.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Guidance on Sound Incentive Compensation Policies</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In 2010, the federal bank regulators jointly issued final guidance on sound incentive compensation policies (&#x201C;SICP&#x201D;) intended to ensure that the incentive compensation policies of banking organizations do not undermine the safety and soundness of such organizations by encouraging excessive risk-taking.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The SICP guidance, which covers all employees that have the ability to materially affect the risk profile of an organization, either individually or as part of a group, is based upon the key principles that a banking organization&#x2019;s incentive compensation arrangements should</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">:</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> (i)</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">provide incentives that do not encourage risk-taking beyond the organization&#x2019;s ability to effectively identify and manage risks, (ii)&nbsp;be compatible with effective internal controls and risk management, and (iii)&nbsp;be supported by strong corporate governance, including active and effective oversight by the organization&#x2019;s board of directors.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Any deficiencies in compensation practices that are identified may be incorporated into the organization&#x2019;s supervisory ratings, which can affect its ability to make acquisitions or perform other actions.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The SICP guidance provides that enforcement actions may be taken against a banking organization if its incentive compensation arrangements or related risk-management control or governance processes pose a risk to the organization&#x2019;s safety and soundness and the organization is not taking prompt and effective measures to correct the deficiencies.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">During the second quarter of 2016, the U.S. financial regulators proposed revised rules on incentive-based payment arrangements at specified regulated entities having at least $1 billion in total assets, including the Company and the Bank. The proposed revised rules would establish general requirements applicable to all covered entities, which would include: (i) prohibiting incentive arrangements that encourage inappropriate risks by providing excessive compensation; (ii) prohibiting incentive arrangements that encourage inappropriate risks that could lead to a material financial loss; (iii) establishing requirements for performance measures to appropriately balance risk and reward; (iv) requiring board of director oversight of incentive arrangements; and (v) mandating appropriate record-keeping. Under the proposed rule, larger financial institutions with total average consolidated assets of at least $50 billion would also be subject to additional requirements applicable to such institutions&#x2019; &#x201C;senior executive officers&#x201D; and &#x201C;significant risk-takers&#x201D;. These additional requirements would not be applicable to the Company which currently has less than $50 billion in total average consolidated assets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Cybersecurity</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:inherit;">In March 2015, the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council issued two related statements regarding cybersecurity. One statement indicates that financial institutions should design multiple layers of security controls to establish lines of defense and to ensure that their risk management processes also address the risk posed by compromised customer credentials, including security measures to reliably authenticate customers accessing internet-based services of the financial institution. The other statement indicates that a financial institution&#x2019;s management is expected to maintain sufficient business continuity planning processes to ensure the rapid recovery, resumption and maintenance of the institution&#x2019;s operations after a cyber-attack involving destructive malware. A financial institution is also </font><font style="display: inline;">expected to develop appropriate processes to enable recovery of data and business operations and address rebuilding network capabilities and restoring data if the institution or its critical service providers fall victim to this type of cyber-attack. If we fail to observe the regulatory guidance, we could be subject to various regulatory sanctions, including financial penalties.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In the ordinary course of business, we rely on electronic communications and information systems to conduct our operations and to store sensitive data. We employ an in-depth, layered, defensive approach that leverages people, processes and technology to manage and maintain cybersecurity controls. We employ a variety of preventative and detective tools to monitor, block, and provide alerts regarding suspicious activity, as well as to report on any suspected advanced persistent threats. Notwithstanding the strength of our defensive measures, the threat from cyber-attacks is severe, attacks are sophisticated and increasing in volume, and attackers respond rapidly to changes in defensive measures. While to date, we have not experienced a significant compromise, significant data loss or any material financial losses related to cybersecurity attacks, our systems and those of our customers and third-party service providers are under constant threat and it is possible that we could experience a significant event in the future. Risks and exposures related to cybersecurity attacks are expected to remain high for the foreseeable future due to the rapidly evolving nature and sophistication of these threats, as well as due to the expanding use of Internet banking, mobile banking and other technology-based products and services by us and our customers. See &#x201C;Risk Factors&#x201D; for a further discussion of risks related to cybersecurity.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;;font-size: 10pt"><a name="Item1A"></a><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;color:#000000;">ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">An investment in our common stock </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">involves </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">risks</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">following is a description of the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">material risks and uncertainties that management believes affect </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">our business and an investment in our common stock. Y</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ou should carefully consider the risks and uncertainties described below together with all of the other information included or incorporated by reference in this report. The risks and uncertainties described below are not the only ones we face. Additional risks and uncertainties that management is not aware of or focused on or that management currently deems immaterial </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">also may become important factors that affect us and</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> our business operations. This report is qualified in its entirety by these risk factors.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> Therefore, the risk factors below should not be considered a complete list of potential risks that we may face.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">If any of the following risks actually occurs, our financial condition, results of operations or cash flows could be materially and adversely affected. If this were to happen, the value of our common stock could decline significantly, and you could lose all or part of your investment.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;color:#000000;">Risks Related to Our Business</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Our loan portfolio exposes us to credit risk.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">There are inherent risks associated with our lending activities</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and we </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">seek to mitigate the</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">se</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> risks by adhering to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">conservative</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> underwriting practices.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Although we believe that our underwriting </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">practices</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> are appropriate for the various kinds of loans we make, we may </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">nevertheless </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">incur losses on loans that meet our underwriting criteria, and these losses may exceed the amounts set aside as reserves in our allowance for loan losses. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Although conditions have improved, difficult </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">economic conditions </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">in the past</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">and the resulting effects on</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> the real estate market</font><font </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">experience</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> a </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">decline in the performance of their loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. This decline was widespread and encompassed a wide variety of loans. Likewise, the value of collateral supporting many of these</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">loans </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">declined </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">over that timeframe,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">and </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">despite market improvement, there can be no assurance that these values will </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">continue to </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">improve</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> or that they will not decline in the future. Accordingly, the deterioration of one or several of these loans could cause a significant increase in nonperforming loans, which could result in a loss of earnings from these loans and an increase in the provision for credit losses and net charge-offs.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">We make both secured and unsecured commercial loans. Unsecured loans generally involve a higher degree of risk of loss than do secured loans because, without collateral, repayment is wholly dependent upon the success of the borrowers&#x2019; respective businesses. Secured commercial loans are generally collateralized by real estate, accounts receivable, inventory, equipment or other assets owned by the borrower and may include a personal guaranty of the business owner. Compared to real estate, other types of collateral securing commercial loans are more difficult to monitor, their values are harder to ascertain, their values may depreciate more rapidly and they may not be as readily saleable if repossessed. Commercial loans secured by collateral other than real estate are generally serviced from the operations of the business, which may not be successful, while commercial real estate loans generally will be serviced from the income on the properties securing the loans. If the Bank&#x2019;s commercial loan portfolio increases, the corresponding risks and potential for losses from these loans will also increase.</font>

As a result, o</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ur earnings</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and cash flows are largely dependent upon our net interest income</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> which</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> is the difference between interest income earned on interest-earning assets such as loans and securities and interest expense paid on interest-bearing liabilities such as deposits and borrowed funds. </font>

If the interest rates paid on deposits and other borrowings increase at a faster rate than the interest rates received on loans and other investments, our net interest income, and therefore </font>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The FDIC, the Federal Reserve and the </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">OCC</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> have promulgated joint guidance on sound risk management practices for financial institutions with concentrations in commercial real estate lending. Under the guidance, a financial institution that, like us, is actively involved in commercial real estate lending should perform a risk assessment to identify concentrations. A financial institution may have a concentration in commercial real estate lending if, among other factors</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">:</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> (i)&nbsp;total reported loans for construction, land development, and other land represent 100% or more of total risk-based capital or (ii)&nbsp;total reported loans </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">for construction, land development and other land and loans secured by multifamily and non-owner occupied non-farm residential properties (excluding loans secured by owner-occupied properties) represent 300% or more of total risk-based capital and the institution&#x2019;s commercial real estate loan portfolio has increased by 50 percent or more during the prior 36 month period</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">. In such event, management should employ heightened risk management practices, including board and management oversight and strategic planning, development of underwriting standards, risk assessment and monitoring through market analysis and stress testing.</font>

In addition, i</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">f we are considered to have a concentration in commercial real estate lending under the foregoing standards in the future and our risk management practices are found to be deficient, it could result in increased reserves and capital costs as well as potential regulatory enforcement action.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Commercial real estate loans are generally viewed as having more inherent risk of default than residential mortgage loans or other consumer loans. Also, the commercial real estate loan balance per borrower is typically larger than that for residential mortgage loans and other consumer loans, inferring higher potential losses on an individual loan basis. The deterioration of one or more of the Bank&#x2019;s significant commercial real estate loans could cause a significant increase in nonaccrual loans. An increase in nonaccrual loans could result in a loss of interest income from these loans, an increase in the provision for loan losses, and an increase in loan charge-offs, all of which could have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">The short-term and long-term impact of the changing regulatory capital requirements and capital rules is unknown. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">In 2013, the FDIC, the OCC and the Federal Reserve Board approved a new rule that substantially amends the regulatory risk-based capital rules applicable to us. The final rule implements the &#x201C;Basel III&#x201D; regulatory capital reforms and changes required by the Dodd-Frank Act. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:24pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The final rule includes minimum risk-based capital and leverage ratios which became effective for us on January 1, 2015, and refines the definition of what constitutes &#x201C;capital&#x201D; for purposes of calculating these ratios. The minimum capital requirements to be considered &#x201C;adequately capitalized&#x201D; are: (i)&nbsp;a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5%; (ii)&nbsp;a Tier 1 to risk-based assets capital ratio of 6.0%, which was increased from 4.0%; (iii)&nbsp;a total capital ratio of 8.0%, which was unchanged from the previous rules; and (iv) a Tier 1 leverage ratio of 4.0%. The final rule also established a &#x201C;capital conservation buffer&#x201D; of 2.5% above the regulatory minimum capital ratios, and when fully effective in 2019, will result in the following minimum capital </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ratios: (</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">a) a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 7.0%; (b) a Tier 1 to risk-based assets capital ratio of 8.5%; and (c) a total capital ratio of 10.5%. The capital conservation buffer requirement began phasing in January 2016 at 0.625% of risk-weighted assets and will increase each year until fully implemented in January 2019. If an institution does not meet or exceed these minimum capital ratios it will be subject to limitations on paying dividends, engaging in share repurchases, and paying discretionary bonuses if its buffer level falls below the required buffer amount. These limitations will establish a maximum percentage of eligible retained income that can be utilized for such activities.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:24pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The application of more stringent capital requirements for us could, among other things, result in lower returns on equity, require the raising of additional capital, and result in regulatory actions such as a prohibition on the payment of dividends, the payment of bonuses to employees or the repurchase of shares if we were unable to comply with such requirements. Furthermore, the imposition of liquidity requirements in connection with the implementation of Basel III could result in our having to restructure our business models or increase our holdings of liquid assets. Implementation of changes in asset risk weightings for risk-based capital calculations, items included or deducted in calculating regulatory capital or additional capital conservation buffers could result in management modifying our business strategy.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.3pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Our allowance for loan losses may not be sufficient to cover actual credit losses, which could adversely affect our earnings and results of operations.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">As a lender, w</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">e &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">are exposed to the risk that our borrowers may not repay their loans according to the terms of these loans and that the collateral securing the payment of a particular loan may be insufficient to fully compensate for the outstanding balance of the loan and the costs to dispose of the underlying collateral. We m</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">aintain an allowance for loan losses, which is a reserve established through a provision for loan losses charged to expense, that </font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">represents management&#x2019;s best estimate of probable incurred losses within </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">our</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> existing portfolio of loans. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Additional credit losses will likely occur in the future and may occur at a rate greater than the Company has experienced to date. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">The level of the allowance reflects management&#x2019;s </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ongoing</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> evaluation of specific credit risks</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> loan loss experience</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> loan portfolio quality</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, economic </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">conditions</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">loan </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">industry concentrations</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and other </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">potential but unidentifiable</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> losses inherent in the current loan portfolio. The determination of the appropriate level of the allowance for loan losses inherently involves a high degree of subjectivity and judgment and requires us to make significant estimates of current credit risks</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">,</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> future trends, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">and general economic conditions, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">all of which may undergo material changes. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Further, the measure of our allowance for loan losses is also dependent on the adoption of new accounting standards. On June 16, 2016, the Financial Accounting Standards Board issued the Current Expected Credit Loss (&#x201C;CECL&#x201D;) standard, which will require financial institutions to estimate and develop a provision for credit losses at origination for the lifetime of the loan, as opposed to reserving for incurred or probable losses up to the balance sheet date. Under the CECL model, credit deterioration would be reflected in the income statement in the period of origination or acquisition of the loan, with changes in expected credit losses due to further credit deterioration or improvement reflected in the periods in which the expectation changes. Accordingly, the CECL model could require financial institutions, such as the Bank, to increase their allowance for loan losses. Moreover, the CECL model could create more volatility in the Bank&#x2019;s level of allowance for loan losses.</font>

A material change to the allowance could cause net income and possibly capital to decrease.</font>

The quarterly surcharge will continue to be assessed until such time as the reserve ratio reaches the statutory minimum of 1.35% required by the Dodd-Frank Act.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;The Company had $</font><font style="display: inline;">3.4 billion</font><font style="display: inline;"> in total assets as of December 31, 2016 and therefore was not subject to the quarterly surcharge.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">At December 31, 2016, the Bank&#x2019;s total assessment rate was approximately three basis points. 		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The market for some of the investment securities held in our portfolio has been volatile over the past several years. Volatile market conditions may </font><font style="display: inline;">quickly and </font><font style="display: inline;">detrimentally affect the value of these securities due to the perception of heightened credit and liquidity risks</font><font style="display: inline;"> associated with their ownership</font><font style="display: inline;">. There can be no assurance that declines in market value will not result in other than temporary impairments of these assets, which would lead to accounting charges that could have a material adverse effect on our net income and capital levels.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">Our accounting estimates and risk management processes rely on analytical and forecasting models.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.3pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Processes that management uses to estimate our probable credit losses and to measure the fair value of financial instruments, as well as the processes used to estimate the effects of changing interest rates and other market measures on our financial condition and results of operations, depend upon the use of analytical and forecasting models. These models reflect assumptions that may not be accurate, particularly in times of market stress or other unforeseen circumstances. Even if these assumptions are accurate, the models may prove to be inadequate or inaccurate because of other flaws in their design or their implementation.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:22.3pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&#xFEFF;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:22.3pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">If the models that management uses for interest rate risk and asset-liability management are inadequate, we may incur increased or unexpected losses upon changes in market interest rates or other market measures. If the models that management uses for determining our probable incurred credit losses are inadequate, the allowance for loan losses may not be sufficient to support future charge-offs. If the models that management uses to measure the fair value of financial instruments are inadequate, the fair value of such financial instruments may fluctuate unexpectedly or may not accurately reflect what we could realize upon sale or settlement of such financial instruments. Any such failure in management&#x2019;s analytical or forecasting models could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;font-size: 10pt">

If any of the information upon which we rely is misrepresented, either fraudulently or inadvertently, and the misrepresentation is not detected prior to asset funding, the value of the asset may be significantly lower than expected, we may fund a loan that we would not have otherwise funded or we may fund a loan on terms that we would not have otherwise extended. Whether a misrepresentation is made by the applicant or by another third party, we generally bear the risk of loss associated with the misrepresentation. A loan subject to a material misrepresentation is typically unsellable or subject to repurchase if it is sold prior to detection of the misrepresentation. The sources of the misrepresentation are often difficult to locate, and it is often difficult to recover any of the monetary losses we may suffer.</font>

The local economic conditions in our market area have a significant impact on our loans, the ability of </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">our </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">borrowers to repay th</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">o</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">se loans and the value of the collateral securing these loans. </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Accordingly, if the population or income growth along the Colorado Front Range is slower than projected, income levels, deposits and housing starts could be adversely affected and could result in a reduction of our expansion, growth and profitability. Any of these events co</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">uld have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">Our business activities and credit exposure are primarily concentrated along the Front Range of Colorado.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> As of December&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">31,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">201</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">6</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">approximately 74% of</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> the book</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> value</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> of our loan portfolio consisted of real estate loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">, the majority of which are secured by properties located in Colorado. A weakening of the real estate market </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">in our primary market areas </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">could have an adverse</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">e</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">ffect </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">on the demand for new loans, the ability of borrowers to repay outstanding loans, the value of real estate and other collateral securing the loans and the value of real estate owned by us. As a result of decreased collateral values, </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">our ability to recover on defaulted loans by selling the underlying real estate </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">would</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> be diminished, and we would be more likely to suffer losses on defaulted loans</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> and a corresponding </font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">material adverse effect on our business, results of operations and financial condition.</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;"> If real estate values decline, it is also more likely that we would be required to increase our allowance for loan losses, which could also adversely affect our business, results of operation and financial condition.</font>

Any one or more of these factors may impair a borrower&#x2019;s ability to repay a loan. In addition, the success of a small to medium-sized business often depends on the management talents and efforts of one or two persons or a small group of persons, and the death, disability or resignation of one or more of these persons could have a material adverse impact on the business and its ability to repay a loan. Economic downturns and other events that negatively impact our market areas could cause us to incur substantial credit losses that could negatively affect our results of operations and financial condition.</font>

We also face competition from many other types of financial institutions, including, without limitation, savings and loans, credit unions, finance companies, brokerage firms, investment advis</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">o</font><font style="display: inline;color:#000000;">rs, insurance companies, factoring companies and other financial intermediaries. 		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;color:#000000;;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:inherit;">Our customers and employees have been, and will continue to be, targeted by parties using fraudulent e-mails and other communications in attempts to misappropriate passwords, bank account information or other personal information or to introduce viruses or other malware through Trojan horse programs to our information systems or our customers&#x2019; computers. Though we endeavor to mitigate these threats through product improvements, use of encryption and authentication technology and customer and employee education, such cyber-attacks against us or our merchants and our third party service providers remain a serious issue. The pervasiveness of cybersecurity incidents in general and the risks of cyber-crime are complex and continue to evolve. More generally, publicized information concerning security and cyber-related problems could inhibit the use or growth of electronic or web-based applications or solutions as a means of conducting commercial transactions.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:inherit;">Although we make significant efforts to maintain the security and integrity of our information systems and have implemented various measures to manage the risk of a security breach or disruption, there can be no assurance that our security efforts and measures will be effective or that attempted security breaches or disruptions would not be successful or damaging. Even the most well protected information, networks, systems and facilities remain potentially vulnerable because attempted security breaches, particularly cyber-attacks and intrusions, or disruptions will occur in the future, and because the techniques used in such attempts are constantly evolving and generally are not recognized until launched against a target, and in some cases are designed not to be detected and, in fact, may not be detected. Accordingly, we may be unable to anticipate these techniques or to implement adequate security barriers or other preventative measures, and thus it is virtually impossible for us to entirely mitigate this risk. While we maintain specific cyber insurance coverage, the amount of coverage may not be adequate in any particular case. Furthermore, because cyber threat scenarios are inherently difficult to predict and can take many forms, some breaches may not be covered under our cyber insurance coverage. A security breach or other significant disruption of our information systems or those related to our customers, merchants and our third party vendors, including as a result of cyber-attacks, could (i)&nbsp;disrupt the proper functioning of our networks and systems and therefore our operations or those of certain of our customers; (ii)&nbsp;result in the unauthorized access to, and destruction, loss, theft, misappropriation or release of confidential, sensitive or otherwise valuable information of ours or our customers; (iii)&nbsp;result in a violation of applicable privacy, data breach and other laws, subjecting us to additional regulatory scrutiny and expose us to civil litigation, governmental fines and possible financial liability; (iv)&nbsp;require significant management attention and resources to remedy the damages that result; or (v)</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:inherit;">harm our reputation or cause a decrease in the number of customers that choose to do business with us. The occurrence of any of the foregoing could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition, cash flows and results of operations.</font>

The effective use of technology increases efficiency and enables financial institutions to better serve customers and reduce costs. Our future success depends, in part, upon our ability to address the needs of our customers by using technology to provide products and services that will satisfy customer demands, as well as create additional efficiencies in our operations. Many of our competitors have substantially greater resources to invest in technological improvements. We may not be able to effectively implement new technology-driven products and services or be successful in marketing these products and services to our customers. Failure to successfully keep pace with technological change affecting the financial services industry could have a material adverse impact on our business and, in turn, our financial condition, results of operations and cash flows.</font>

For example, consumers can now maintain funds that would have historically been held as bank deposits in brokerage accounts, mutual funds or general-purpose reloadable prepaid cards. Consumers can also complete transactions such as paying bills</font><font style="display: inline;">, obtaining a loan</font><font style="display: inline;"> or transferring funds directly without the assistance of a bank. The process of eliminating banks as intermediaries, or &#x201C;disintermediation,&#x201D; could result in the loss of fee income, as well as the loss of customer deposits and the related income generated from those deposits. The loss of these revenue streams and the lower cost of deposits as a source of funds could have a material adverse effect on our financial condition, cash flows and results of operations.</font>
